questions.q: In the glossary, what does MOL (Middle of Line) refer to?
options: The 15-18 copper/low-k interconnect levels built after the first contact level
The contact levels between the transistors and M1: trench silicide, source/drain contacts (W, Co, or Ru), gate contacts, and M0
The mid-wafer inspection point between FEOL and BEOL where WAT parametric tests are run
The middle deck of a string-stacked 3D NAND array
questions.explanation: MOL is the set of contact levels that connect the FEOL transistors to the first true BEOL wiring level. The copper/low-k stack above it is the BEOL; WAT is an end-of-line parametric test, not a process stage.

questions.q: Using the sense-of-scale table, order these from largest to smallest: the tightest N3/N2 metal pitch, the contacted poly pitch, the EUV wavelength, and a killer particle.
options: EUV wavelength > metal pitch > killer particle > contacted poly pitch
Metal pitch > EUV wavelength > contacted poly pitch > killer particle
Killer particle > contacted poly pitch > metal pitch > EUV wavelength
Contacted poly pitch (~45-48 nm) > killer particle (~20-30 nm) roughly equal to metal pitch (~23-25 nm) > EUV wavelength (13.5 nm)
questions.explanation: CPP is ~45-48 nm, the tightest metal pitch is ~23-25 nm, a killer particle is anything larger than about half the metal pitch (~20-30 nm), and the EUV wavelength is 13.5 nm. The scanner prints features larger than its wavelength only by virtue of k1 near 0.3 and NA 0.33-0.55.

questions.q: The node table shows contacted poly pitch (CPP) essentially flat at ~45-50 nm from TSMC N5 through N2 and A16. Why, and where does remaining density gain come from?
options: CPP must fit a gate, two spacers, and a contact, so it has hit a physical floor; density now comes from metal-pitch scaling, cell-height reduction (fewer tracks, backside power), and DTCO
CPP is limited by the 0.33 NA EUV resolution of ~13.5 nm, so only High-NA tools can shrink it; density gains come from FinFET fin count
Foundries deliberately hold CPP constant so PDKs remain compatible across nodes; density comes from larger reticles
CPP stopped scaling because copper resistivity rises sharply below 50 nm; density now comes from stacking two logic dies with SoIC
questions.explanation: A gate pitch has to contain the gate length, two dielectric spacers, and a source/drain contact, and each of those has stopped shrinking. Since N5 the density gain per node (~1.15-1.3x) has come from metal pitch, track reduction, backside power delivery, and design-technology co-optimization such as SDB and COAG.

questions.q: According to the node table and its commentary, what happened to wafer price and lithography's share of cost between TSMC N5 and N2?
options: Wafer price fell from ~$30k to ~$16-17k as EUV matured, and litho's share dropped to ~25%
Wafer price stayed at ~$10k while EUV layer count fell from ~25 to ~14
Wafer price rose from ~$16-17k (N5) to ~$30k (N2) as EUV layers went from ~14 to ~25+, and litho's share of wafer cost grew from ~25% at N16 to ~35-40% at N2
Wafer price rose to ~$30k solely because N2 uses High-NA EUV on every critical layer
questions.explanation: The table lists N5 at ~$16-17k with ~14 EUV layers and N2 at ~$30k with ~25+ EUV layers including EUV LELE on M0 and vias. Each EUV layer costs 2-3x a DUV layer in tool time, so litho's share climbed from ~25% at N16 to ~35-40% at N2, and cost per transistor stopped falling.

questions.q: The glossary defines Little's law as WIP = throughput x cycle time. A fab running 100,000 wafer starts per month with a 90-day cycle time carries roughly how many wafers in process?
options: ~100,000 wafers, one month's worth
~300,000 wafers, three months' worth
~900,000 wafers, since each wafer passes through ~9 re-entrant loops
~30,000 wafers, since lots of 25 are counted as single units
questions.explanation: 100,000 wafers per month times a 3-month (90-day) cycle time gives ~300,000 wafers in process at any moment. Re-entrant flow explains why the cycle time is 90 days for 1,000-1,500 steps but does not multiply the WIP count.

questions.q: The glossary lists three die-yield models. Which statement correctly matches them?
options: Poisson is the industry default; Murphy is the most pessimistic; negative binomial ignores defect clustering
Negative binomial is the most pessimistic; Poisson includes a clustering parameter alpha; Murphy is used only for memory
Murphy Y = e^(-A*D0) is the simplest; Poisson uses the squared bracket form; both assume clustering

Poisson Y = e^(-A*D0) is the simplest and most pessimistic; Murphy Y = [(1 - e^(-A*D0))/(A*D0)]^2 is less pessimistic for large dies; negative binomial Y = (1 + A*D0/alpha)^(-alpha) with alpha ~2-5 accounts for clustering and is the industry default
questions.explanation: Poisson assumes random, unclustered defects and gives the lowest yield; Murphy softens it for large dies; the negative binomial adds a clustering parameter alpha (typically 2-5) and is what foundries actually use. All three take die area A and killer defect density D0 (~0.05-0.1 /cm2 at a mature leading node) as inputs.
